Advanced security configuration

Source: vignettes/advanced-security.Rmd
advanced-security.Rmd

Overview

Some login providers require extra proof that a request comes from your app, or extra protection for the tokens they issue. Start with the working app in Usage, then configure the features your provider requires.

A signature lets the receiver check who sent a message and whether it changed. Encryption hides its contents. A client certificate or signing key can also tie an access token to your app, so the token alone is not enough to use it.

Choose the feature your provider requires; enabling every extension is not necessary. Both the provider and the API must support the selected behavior.

Need Feature
Prove the app’s identity with a signing key JWT client authentication
Present a registered certificate Mutual TLS
Send request details directly to the provider PAR
Sign the login request JAR
Return login results outside the URL or with a signature Form Post or JARM
Require a matching key when using a token DPoP

Examples use placeholder addresses and key files. Replace them with your registered values and keep private keys on the server.

Provider metadata and OIDC discovery

Discovery reads the provider’s published settings so you do not have to copy each endpoint and supported feature manually:

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = "https://id.example.com"
)

Published support does not configure your individual app registration. Select the authentication method and credentials agreed with your provider.

JWT client authentication

With private_key_jwt, your app signs a short-lived JSON Web Token (JWT) when requesting tokens instead of sending a shared secret. Register the public key with the provider, then configure the matching private key:

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  "https://id.example.com", token_auth_style = "private_key_jwt"
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider = provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile"),
  client_assertion_private_key = openssl::read_key("keys/client-key.pem"),
  client_assertion_private_key_kid = "registered-key-id"
)

The provider uses the public key to verify the app’s message. For secret-based assertions, see oauth_client(). See endpoint-specific authentication for credentials and audience settings.

Mutual TLS (mTLS)

mTLS lets your app present a certificate during the secure network connection. It can identify the app to the provider. Separately, a provider can issue certificate-bound tokens that an API accepts only with the matching certificate. Configure the use agreed with your provider:

provider <- oauth_provider(
  name = "example-mtls",
  # Exact OIDC issuer; enables nonce and ID-token validation
  issuer = "https://id.example.com",
  auth_url = "https://id.example.com/authorize",
  token_url = "https://id.example.com/token",
  jwks_uri = "https://id.example.com/jwks",
  userinfo_url = "https://id.example.com/userinfo",
  # Use RFC 8705 client-certificate auth at the token endpoint
  token_auth_style = "tls_client_auth",
  # Use mTLS-specific endpoints when the provider publishes them
  mtls_endpoint_aliases = list(
    token_endpoint = "https://mtls.id.example.com/token",
    userinfo_endpoint = "https://mtls.id.example.com/userinfo"
  ),
  # Expect certificate-bound access tokens from the provider
  mtls_client_certificate_bound_access_tokens = TRUE
)
client <- oauth_client(
  provider = provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/auth/callback",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile"),
  # Certificate and key sent on mTLS requests
  mtls_client_cert_file = "certs/client.pem",
  mtls_client_key_file = "certs/client-key.pem",
  mtls_client_ca_file = "certs/ca.pem",
  # Require the matching certificate when access tokens are used
  mtls_certificate_bound_access_tokens = TRUE
)

Certificate files alone do not enable certificate-bound tokens; the example selects that policy explicitly. The default also requires shinyOAuth to observe and verify the token’s certificate binding. If your provider uses opaque tokens, see the certificate-binding details below.

On Windows, separate PEM certificate and key files require curl’s OpenSSL backend. Follow the platform setup in that section before testing mTLS.

Pushed authorization requests (PAR)

PAR sends login-request details directly from your server to the provider. The browser carries a short reference instead of the full request, which keeps most details out of browser history and avoids very long URLs.

provider <- oauth_provider(
  name = "example-par",
  issuer = "https://id.example.com",
  auth_url = "https://id.example.com/authorize",
  token_url = "https://id.example.com/token",
  # Enable pushed authorization requests
  par_url = "https://id.example.com/par",
  par_required = TRUE,
  # Keep the browser redirect down to client_id + PAR request_uri
  authorization_request_front_channel_mode = "minimal"
)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider = provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  client_secret = "client-secret",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/auth/callback",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile")
)

Use the provider’s published PAR endpoint. par_required = TRUE records its requirement; it does not enable PAR on the provider’s server.

JWT-secured authorization request (JAR)

JAR signs the login request so the provider can detect changes to its parameters. You can combine it with PAR. Register the signing key and check that the provider requires signed requests for this app; a local setting cannot prevent the provider from accepting unsigned requests.

provider <- oauth_provider(
  name = "example-jar",
  issuer = "https://id.example.com",
  auth_url = "https://id.example.com/authorize",
  token_url = "https://id.example.com/token",
  # The server registration must already require signed Request Objects
  signed_request_object_required = TRUE,
  request_parameter_supported = TRUE,
  request_object_signing_alg_values_supported = c("RS256")
)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider = provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  client_secret = "client-secret",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/auth/callback",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile"),
  # Signing key for the Request Object
  client_assertion_private_key = openssl::read_key("keys/client-key.pem"),
  # Send the authorization request as a JWT in the request parameter
  request_object_mode = "request",
  request_object_signing_alg = "RS256"
)

Test both an accepted signed request and rejection of an otherwise valid unsigned request before deployment. The rejection must be for the missing signature, not an unrelated configuration error. See the test request below.

If your provider fetches signed requests from the app, see Request Objects published by the Shiny app.

Form Post response mode

Form Post returns the login result in an HTTP request body instead of the browser URL. Use it when your provider requires that transport or when callback values should stay out of browser history. It does not sign or encrypt the result.

Set response_mode = "form_post" on the client, then use the matching wrapper:

base_ui <- shiny::fluidPage(shiny::textOutput("status"))
ui <- oauth_form_post_ui(base_ui, id = "auth", client = client)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server("auth", client)
  output[["status"]] <- shiny::renderText({
    if (isTRUE(auth[["authenticated"]])) "Signed in" else "Waiting for login"
  })
}

app <- shiny::shinyApp(ui, server, uiPattern = ".*")

Keep the module ID and client the same in UI and server. uiPattern = ".*" allows Shiny to serve a dedicated callback path.

If your proxy accepts HTTPS but forwards HTTP to Shiny, the wrapper needs a trusted way to recover the public callback address. See the HTTPS proxy example below.

JWT-secured authorization response mode (JARM)

JARM signs the returning login result. shinyOAuth verifies it before accepting the callback fields, giving the app a way to check the response’s sender and integrity. Select the mode and signing algorithm supported by your registration:

provider <- oauth_provider(
  name = "example-jarm",
  issuer = "https://id.example.com",
  auth_url = "https://id.example.com/authorize",
  token_url = "https://id.example.com/token",
  # Advertise the JARM response modes and algorithms this provider supports
  response_modes_supported = c("query", "query.jwt", "form_post.jwt"),
  jarm_signing_alg_values_supported = c("RS256"),
  jarm_encryption_alg_values_supported = c("RSA-OAEP"),
  jarm_encryption_enc_values_supported = c("A128CBC-HS256")
)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider = provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  client_secret = "client-secret",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/auth/callback",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile"),
  # Ask for a JWT-wrapped authorization response
  response_mode = "query.jwt",
  jarm_signed_response_alg = "RS256"
)

JARM uses oauth_module_server(). With form_post.jwt, also use oauth_form_post_ui(). Optional response encryption requires additional client settings and support for local R subprocesses; see the encrypted response example below.

Demonstrating proof-of-possession (DPoP)

DPoP ties an access token to a signing key. Each request includes fresh proof that the app holds that key, so an API enforcing DPoP cannot accept a stolen token on its own. The provider and the API must both support it.

provider <- oauth_provider(
  name = "example-dpop",
  issuer = "https://id.example.com",
  auth_url = "https://id.example.com/authorize",
  token_url = "https://id.example.com/token",
  # Optional metadata check for acceptable DPoP signing algorithms
  dpop_signing_alg_values_supported = c("ES256")
)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider = provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  client_secret = "client-secret",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/auth/callback",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "api.read"),
  # Private key used to sign DPoP proofs
  dpop_private_key = openssl::read_key("keys/dpop-key.pem"),
  dpop_signing_alg = "ES256"
)

After login, let the request helper attach the proof and handle provider nonce challenges:

resp <- perform_resource_req(
  auth[["token"]],
  "https://api.example.com/me",
  # Lets shinyOAuth attach the DPoP proof and handle nonce challenges
  client = client
)

Use the final trusted API URL and keep redirects disabled. For tokens tied to a key or certificate, use the request helpers with client = client rather than passing a bare token string to another package.

Browser binding and deployment boundary

Use HTTPS, finish login in the tab that started it, and keep cookies and session storage available. Host the app separately from untrusted services: cookies are shared across ports on a hostname, and scripts on the app’s own origin can read its session storage. Protect the app against injected scripts and keep callback queries out of proxy logs.

Use oauth_ui() or oauth_form_post_ui() with the matching module ID and client. They handle callbacks before loading application UI. Custom integrations using prepare_call() and handle_callback() must establish their own browser binding.

Endpoint-specific authentication

For the client assertion profile referenced by OAuth 2.1 draft 16, use the trusted issuer as the audience and optionally select the recommended type:

client@client_assertion_audience <- provider@issuer
client@client_assertion_typ <- "client-authentication+jwt"

RFC7523bis draft 11 section 4 describes these settings. They apply to client authentication assertions, not JAR, JARM or ID token headers. Match them to your provider’s registration.

PAR, introspection and revocation can each require different authentication:

client@endpoint_auth <- list(
  introspection = list(
    token_auth_style = "header",
    client_id = "registered-inspector",
    client_secret = Sys.getenv("INTROSPECTION_SECRET"),
    extra_headers = c("X-App" = "registered-app")
  ),
  revocation = list(
    token_auth_style = "private_key_jwt",
    client_assertion_private_key = openssl::read_key("keys/revocation-key.pem"),
    client_assertion_alg = "RS256",
    client_assertion_audience = "https://id.example.com/revocation"
  )
)

Unspecified credentials inherit the client settings. Confirm each endpoint’s method and audience with your provider. extra_token_headers applies only to exchange and refresh; use extra_headers to send headers to other endpoints.

Certificate binding and platform requirements

mtls_certificate_bound_access_tokens = TRUE enables certificate presentation and mTLS endpoint selection, independently of the client authentication method. Certificate files alone do not enable it.

By default, mtls_require_observed_cnf = TRUE requires visible binding data that matches the certificate. Some providers use opaque tokens whose binding only their servers can check. For that agreed deployment, keep certificate-bound requests enabled and allow missing local confirmation:

client <- oauth_client(
  provider = provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/auth/callback",
  mtls_client_cert_file = "certs/client.pem",
  mtls_client_key_file = "certs/client-key.pem",
  mtls_certificate_bound_access_tokens = TRUE,
  mtls_require_observed_cnf = FALSE
)

shinyOAuth still presents the certificate and rejects any observed mismatch. The provider and API must enforce binding; see RFC 8705 section 3.

On Windows, separate PEM certificate/key files require curl’s OpenSSL backend. Set CURL_SSL_BACKEND=openssl in .Renviron and restart R before loading curl, httr2 or shinyOAuth. Check the active backend with curl::curl_version()[["ssl_version"]]; shinyOAuth rejects Schannel for this configuration. See the curl certificate guide.

For dynamic registration, oauth_client_mtls_registration() builds the matching certificate registration metadata.

Testing signed-request enforcement

Test the server policy with an otherwise valid request for the same client that omits the signed Request Object:

unsigned <- httr2::request(provider@auth_url) |>
  httr2::req_url_query(
    client_id = client@client_id,
    redirect_uri = client@redirect_uri,
    response_type = "code", scope = "openid profile",
    state = "unsigned-policy-probe",
    code_challenge = "E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM",
    code_challenge_method = "S256"
  ) |>
  httr2::req_options(followlocation = FALSE) |>
  httr2::req_error(is_error = function(resp) FALSE) |>
  httr2::req_perform()
httr2::resp_status(unsigned)
httr2::resp_headers(unsigned)
httr2::resp_body_string(unsigned)

Confirm rejection specifically because the signed object is missing. A generic HTTP error, login page or login_required response does not prove enforcement. Test this alongside a successful signed request.

To encrypt the signed request, select supported request_object_encryption_alg and request_object_encryption_enc values, and configure a provider encryption key. See oauth_client() and oauth_provider(). PAR can also carry the signed object while keeping most details out of the URL.

Request Objects published by the Shiny app

With request_object_mode = "request_uri", shinyOAuth publishes the signed request at a short-lived URL for the provider to fetch. This differs from PAR, where the provider issues the reference. Prefer PAR when supported; app-hosted Request Objects cannot be used when the provider requires PAR.

The provider must be able to reach the public HTTPS URL. Register it or its prefix if your provider requires this:

request_uri_provider <- oauth_provider(
  name = "example-request-uri",
  issuer = "https://id.example.com",
  auth_url = "https://id.example.com/authorize",
  token_url = "https://id.example.com/token",
  request_uri_parameter_supported = TRUE,
  request_object_signing_alg_values_supported = "RS256"
)

client <- oauth_client(
  provider = request_uri_provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  client_secret = "client-secret",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/auth/callback",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile"),
  client_assertion_private_key = openssl::read_key("keys/client-key.pem"),
  # Publish the Request Object by reference instead of sending it inline
  request_object_mode = "request_uri",
  request_object_signing_alg = "RS256"
)

# Inside server()
auth <- oauth_module_server(
  "auth",
  client,
  auto_redirect = TRUE,
  # Public HTTPS base URL of this Shiny app as seen by the provider
  request_uri_base_url = "https://shiny.yourdomain.com/myapp"
)

Use oauth_ui() or oauth_form_post_ui() with the same client and state store as the server. Multiple R processes need a shared store with atomic take(); see custom_cache().

Treat retrieval URLs as secrets: anyone holding a live handle can consume the object. Signing leaves its claims readable, so encrypt it if those claims need confidentiality and protect the stored record. Keep URLs out of logs.

The "minimal" front-channel mode is for compatible PAR providers; it is not available for OIDC inline or app-hosted signed requests.

Deployment behind an HTTPS proxy

If your web server accepts HTTPS but forwards HTTP to Shiny, the wrapper needs a trusted way to recover the public request address. Configure request_uri_resolver for your own proxy. This example accepts one proxy IP and a fixed public origin, including a mounted app path:

trusted_proxy_uri <- function(req) {
  if (!identical(req[["REMOTE_ADDR"]], "10.0.0.10") ||
      !identical(req[["HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO"]], "https")) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  paste0("https://app.example.com", req[["SCRIPT_NAME"]], req[["PATH_INFO"]])
}

ui <- oauth_form_post_ui(
  base_ui, id = "auth", client = client,
  request_uri_resolver = trusted_proxy_uri
)

Use your deployment’s verified proxy address and public origin. The result must still match the configured redirect origin and callback path. Do not trust forwarded headers from arbitrary clients.

Encrypted authorization responses

For encrypted JARM, add the decryption settings:

client <- oauth_client(
  provider = provider,
  client_id = "client-id",
  client_secret = "client-secret",
  redirect_uri = "https://app.example.com/auth/callback",
  scopes = c("openid", "profile"),
  response_mode = "query.jwt",
  jarm_signed_response_alg = "RS256",
  # Optional: decrypt JARM before validating the signed payload
  jarm_encrypted_response_alg = "RSA-OAEP",
  jarm_encrypted_response_enc = "A128CBC-HS256",
  jarm_decryption_private_key = openssl::read_key("keys/jarm-decrypt.pem")
)

Use oauth_module_server() and, for form_post.jwt, oauth_form_post_ui(). Encrypted callbacks use a temporary local R process, so hosting must permit subprocesses and allow for startup time. The decrypted response still needs signature and login-state validation.

Token binding requirements and validation

With a DPoP key configured, dpop_require_access_token defaults to TRUE. The provider must return a DPoP token, and any visible key binding must match. Use dpop_require_observed_cnf = TRUE if local confirmation is required; opaque tokens may need introspection to provide it.

Certificate-bound tokens similarly need matching certificate data. Refresh must provide fresh binding data; shinyOAuth does not reuse the old certificate thumbprint when the new response omits it. Malformed binding data is rejected.

Reading binding data from a JWT access token does not verify that token’s signature. Introspection can confirm it with the provider. The API must also enforce binding for a stolen token to be unusable without its key or certificate.

DPoP in API requests

perform_resource_req() and get_userinfo() handle a nonce challenge with one fresh-proof retry. Keep redirects disabled and use the trusted final URL: the proof is tied to the request’s method and address.

Pass query parameters through query and avoid modifying a prepared request’s URL or method. Use perform_resource_req() to retain nonce handling and decoded response-size limits; direct httr2::req_perform() uses httr2’s transport. If your provider issues unusually large nonces, see shinyOAuth.dpop_nonce_max_bytes in package options.

Policy identity across callbacks and retained credentials

Pending logins and saved connections remember the client and provider policies that created them. Policy changes invalidate those records. After upgrades that change the policy encoding, users must sign in again; update workers that share keys and storage together.

If a custom userinfo_id_selector depends on external settings, assign a userinfo_id_selector_policy_id and change it when those settings or helper behavior change. Keep them stable while the client is in use. The Spotify helper tracks its allow_legacy_id setting automatically.

Issuer comparison and transport policy

Keep callback issuer checks enabled. compare_callback_issuer = TRUE compares iss exactly with the trusted provider@issuer; enforce_callback_issuer also requires it to be present. Providers advertising RFC 9207 support require the identifier, while validated JARM supplies its own issuer. Apps using several providers still need issuer identification or distinct callback routes.

For legacy providers that omit iss, configure comparison and presence policy explicitly rather than disabling checks to bypass an error. See oauth_client().

Package HTTPS requests require TLS 1.2 or later by default. options(shinyOAuth.tls_min_version = "1.3") selects a higher minimum; set it before discovery or login. Browser and proxy TLS need separate configuration. See package options.

Callback pages and application scripts

Use oauth_ui(ui, id = "auth", client = client) for query and query-JARM callbacks, with the same ID and client as oauth_module_server(). The wrapper processes callbacks before loading application UI and sets privacy headers.

Configure hosting and proxy logs to omit callback queries; response headers cannot remove upstream logs. Keep third-party scripts off unsanitized callback pages, including custom integrations using use_shinyOAuth().

Register fixed routing query parameters in the redirect URI; continuation discards unregistered inbound parameters. Behind a trusted HTTPS proxy, configure request_uri_resolver using the trust checks described for oauth_form_post_ui().

Provider key-set validation

shinyOAuth checks the entire provider key set before selecting a signing key. A malformed entry can therefore interrupt login or signed responses even if another key would work. Providers must publish valid entries throughout key rotation; see RFC 7517 section 5 for the standard’s less restrictive recommendation.

Each RSA key must use one signing algorithm, including when reused under different key IDs. Rotate the key when changing algorithms, update related pins and settings, and coordinate workers and caches. Changing only kid does not change the key. See oauth_provider() for pinning and key-selection settings.

Trusted ID-token audiences

ID tokens with multiple audiences remain rejected by default. If an issuer legitimately includes another trusted audience, configure trusted_id_token_audiences = c("trusted-service") on oauth_client(). The token must still include this client’s ID in aud, and azp must equal this client’s ID when present. Trusted multiple audiences do not require an azp claim under OIDC Core section 3.1.3.7. Other audiences, incorrect authorized parties, and invalid signatures are rejected.

Signature and encryption support

Choose an algorithm supported by both the provider and shinyOAuth. The outgoing signing defaults depend on the key; RSA defaults to RS256, so select client_assertion_alg = "RS384" explicitly when the registration requires it.

Use Supported algorithms
Private-key assertions, JAR and DPoP RS256, RS384, ES256, ES384, ES512, and EdDSA or Ed25519 with Ed25519 keys.
Secret-based assertions and JAR HS256, HS384, HS512.
Request Object encryption and JARM decryption RSA-OAEP with A128CBC-HS256, A192CBC-HS384 or A256CBC-HS512.

Outgoing RSA-PSS and Ed448 signatures are unsupported. For encryption, RSA-OAEP-256 and GCM JWE modes are unsupported, as are encrypted ID tokens and encrypted UserInfo. Unsupported metadata does not trigger a fallback algorithm.

Incoming signature policies are separate. See oauth_provider() and the jarm_* settings in oauth_client().
